title: Identifying the Talent You Cannot See
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The problem this piece names is a blind spot rather than a judgement error: capable people working in other parts of the organisation, or in junior or specialised roles, who sustain a record of excellence entirely below a given leader's radar. It treats knowing where talent sits across the enterprise as part of the job, then asks the obvious practical question of how that is possible for people one never encounters. The answer offered is a conversational habit, closing exchanges with peers and colleagues with a short set of standing questions about who is doing great work, who is making an impression, and who should be on the radar. The piece notes that this works because colleagues are already interested in the same information and share it readily. The step after collection is the one that pays: reaching out to recognise those named, since hearing that senior people are hearing good things has a material effect on motivation. The risk it closes on is concrete, that unrecognised and undeveloped franchise players leave, and that failing to extend opportunity puts a ceiling on what the organisation can do.
points: The problem is framed as a visibility failure rather than a judgement failure, since sustained excellence in another part of the organisation simply never reaches a given leader.
The mechanism is a habit rather than a process, ending peer conversations with standing questions about who is doing great work and who should be on the radar.
It works because the information is already circulating: colleagues want to know where the talent is and share it freely once asked.
The follow-through is where the value sits, since hearing that senior people are hearing good things measurably lifts motivation.
The stated risk is losing franchise players who were never recognised or developed, and capping the organisation by not extending opportunity to top talent.
quotes: Too often, these colleagues do impressive work and sustain a record of excellence but fall below your radar.
Yet, one of the jobs of every leader is to know where the talent resides throughout the enterprise.
Because the best leaders are all about talent, wherever it may be, their antennae are always fixed on learning about who is doing great things they can’t see.
When people hear that those more senior to them are hearing “good things,” this has a material effect on their motivation to do even more.
Leaders who don’t know the talent beyond their immediate team take the chance of losing such talent because they aren’t recognized or developed.
Moreover, they know that without giving top talent even more opportunity, they are putting a ceiling on what is possible.
